title: Israel Asks for a King
english: Israel gave up being ruled by God as their king through the prophets, and called for a man as king. For this very reason they also slipped from the commandment: for Solomon was the first to worship the Baals (1 Kings 11:5–8), and then after him Jeroboam set up the heifers (1 Kings 12:28–29).

“And the Lord said to Samuel, ‘Listen to their voice,’” and so on (1 Samuel 8:22). Though their affairs were going well for them and were set in the best of order, the wretched people planned bitter things against themselves. Shaking off, as it were, the yoke of the kingdom under God, they came to the blessed Samuel, saying: “Appoint a king over us to judge us” (1 Samuel 8:5), and the rest. Then, when the blessed Samuel announced to them the rights of the king (1 Samuel 8:11–18), filling them with many terrors, and very earnestly trying to turn them away…
translator_notes: Catena sigla '{Κυρίλλου.}' (of Cyril) are not rendered in the reading text; the first comment answers the lemma 1 Samuel 8:5 at the end of the previous section.
The column number 69.681 inside the text is not rendered.
'δαμάλεις' rendered 'heifers', as in the LXX of 3 Kingdoms 12:28; English Bibles say 'calves'.
The last sentence breaks off mid-clause at the section boundary and continues in the next section; marked with an ellipsis.
baehrens: PG 69; Fragmenta in Regum b01 rem early

title: Repaying a Kindness; Doeg the Edomite
english: …from such rotten and unholy designs, they clung to their demand no less, saying: “No, but there shall be a king over us” (1 Samuel 8:19).

“And Saul said to his servant,” and so on; “And what shall we bring?” and so on (1 Samuel 9:7). (Cyril, from his Commentary on Matthew.) It is always natural for those who have been helped, that is, who have received very pleasant things from others, to want to make whatever return they can, and to gladden their benefactors with equal or even greater honors. And those in whom a good and grateful character is present always show, in one way or another, their eagerness in these things as proof of their gratitude.
“And one of Saul’s servants was there, and his name was Doeg” (1 Samuel 21:7). There was a certain man, an Edomite by race, whose name was Doeg. This man lived among the guards of…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, continuing the last sentence of the previous section.
The quoted reply has βασιλεία ('kingship') where the LXX has βασιλεύς; rendered with the familiar sense 'there shall be a king over us'.
The siglum 'Κυρίλλου, ἐκ τοῦ κατὰ Ματθαῖον' names a different source work (the Commentary on Matthew) and is kept as a short parenthesis; the plain '{Κυρίλλου.}' sigla are not rendered.
'ὑπὸ τῶν τυχόντων ἡδίστων μετεσχηκόσιν' rendered by sense, 'who have received very pleasant things from others'.

'ἀπεστρέφετο παρὰ τοῖς δορυφόροις' is hard as printed ('turned away among the guards'); it is rendered as if it were ἀνεστρέφετο ('lived among'), which fits the following account of Doeg spying on David. This is a conjecture.
The last sentence breaks off at the section boundary and continues in the next section.
baehrens: PG 69; Fragmenta in Regum b01 rem mid

title: Doeg Betrays David
english: …the blessed David. He was a herdsman, but a bitter and barbarous man, with nothing genuine about him at all. He used to meet Saul in secret and report to him David’s deliberations and all his plans, and he promised that in due time he would also hand him over. And once, having seen the blessed David enter the house of God, when he ate the bread of the Presence, and meet Ahimelech the priest (1 Samuel 21:1–6), he reported to Saul that David had only a very few men with him, and that Saul could easily seize him by coming upon him, and overpower him without trouble (1 Samuel 22:9–10).
So Doeg betrayed him by reporting to Saul that he had met Ahimelech in the house of God; but the Master of all kept the prophet safe, and brought that perverse man’s attempt to nothing.
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, completing the last sentence of the previous section.
'Ἀβιμέλεχ' is the LXX form; rendered 'Ahimelech', the name English Bibles use for the priest of Nob.
'τοὺς ἄρτους τῆς προθέσεως' rendered 'the bread of the Presence', the standard English name for the holy bread.
'David' is supplied twice where the Greek leaves the person unstated ('David’s deliberations', 'David had only a very few men'); no content is added.
'ὁ τῶν ὅλων Δεσπότης' rendered 'the Master of all'; David is called 'the prophet' as in the Greek.
baehrens: PG 69; Fragmenta in Regum b01 rem close
